title: Louis Armstrong's influence and the trumpet lineage
summary: Davenport says he phrased like Armstrong on his solo, and traces trumpet influence through Eldridge, Gillespie, Miles Davis and Parker.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Now, the reason why I like this book, I've never heard Louis Armstrong play it. But I can always hear him with my mind's ear playing this. Because it sounds like he should have played this number. And if you notice, on my chorus, I play some of his licks. Not many of his exact licks. In other words, I play, I phrase the way he would have phrased it. On spots. Not all the way through my solo. But some spots on my solo I phrase it. Was he any good? Oh, Louis Armstrong? Yes, he did. He said the style, he said the triumph of modern trumpet playing.
You don't think he was just a clown?

No, indeed not. No, indeed. Often, what would trumpet playing be like today had it not been for Louis Armstrong? Yes. See, because Roy Eldridge got his inspiration from Ray Allen and Louis Armstrong. Which Ray Allen got his inspiration for Louis Armstrong. Dizzy Gillespie got his from Roy Eldridge. Miles Davis got his from...
Dizzy Gillespie. And he went on up to Freddie Hubbard. You know, I think those guys listen to Lester, too. Yeah. Because they get a cool sound like Lester Young.
Yeah, well, not one guy. I think he really got his thing. Dizzy Gillespie.
He got a lot of interest.

Yeah, yeah. Well, all those guys got a lot of interest. Parker, look, he helped them. I don't care what they said. They helped him, maybe, too. But you know how old Miles was playing with Parker? Yeah. He was just a child.
He was about 18 to 19 years old.
I think Miles Davis was about 20... He must have been about 20 or 21 when he was playing with Parker.
I think Parker helped him when he was just a kid. Because he came to Juilliard quite young. And then he got tired of that job. I mean, that wonderful music school.
